country.comment: Single-country empirical study examining rural small-scale piped water supply systems across municipalities in Brazil.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title and Summary; PDF p. 3, Section 2

effect_estimate.comment: Exact quantitative estimates from municipal panel DiD and kernel-matched DiD regressions (2000–2010), plus accountability channel interactions. Note that in Table 6 Panel A col. 3–4, the PDF font dropped minus signs on mayoral victory margin coefficients, which Section 6 text (PDF p. 12) explicitly states are negative.
effect_estimate.value: In kernel-matched difference-in-differences regressions (2000–2010; N = 1,008 municipalities / 1,899 municipality-year observations), small-scale rural water supply systems implemented and managed by community water user associations (+assoc) increased rural household piped water access rates by 6.58 percentage points more than systems implemented and managed by local governments (b = 0.0658, SE = 0.0161, p < 0.01 clustered by municipality; SE = 0.0271, p < 0.05 clustered by state; bootstrapped difference = 0.0659, SE = 0.0237, p < 0.01, N = 955; unweighted FE on matched sample b = 0.0772, SE = 0.0134, p < 0.01). Descriptively, rural piped water access rose from 16.0% in 2000 to 33.4% in 2010 (+17.4 percentage points, N = 583) in user-association municipalities versus from 15.3% to 24.9% (+9.6 percentage points, N = 592) in local-government municipalities (raw difference = 7.9 percentage points, p < 0.01). Against municipalities with no new rural project (N = 5,344 municipalities / 9,928 observations with covariates), user-association projects increased rural piped water access by 6.67 percentage points (b = 0.0667, SE = 0.00987, p < 0.01), whereas local-government projects had no statistically significant effect above the national trend (b = 0.00662, SE = 0.00614). Urban placebo (b = 0.00391, SE = 0.0120) and 1990–2000 pre-trend checks (b = 0.0144, SE = 0.0191) were null. Within local-government project municipalities (N = 520–522), rural access gains were significantly larger where a social group had requested a water system in 2000 (+7.93 percentage points, b = 0.0793, SE = 0.0231, p < 0.01), where user participation mechanisms existed in 2008 (+4.09 percentage points, b = 0.0409, SE = 0.0165, p < 0.05), where local TV (+10.4 percentage points, b = 0.104, SE = 0.0234, p < 0.01) or radio (+4.08 percentage points, b = 0.0408, SE = 0.0204, p < 0.10) existed, and where 2004 mayoral victory margins were narrower (magnitude 0.150, SE = 0.0594, p < 0.05, negative in text), whereas none of these political accountability channels affected user-association municipalities (N = 506–507).

mechanism_certainty.comment: Quasi-experimental study appraised with ROBINS-I at Moderate overall risk of bias: municipal fixed effects / DiD remove time-invariant confounding, multinomial probit kernel matching balances baseline and pre-treatment covariates (<20% standardized bias across covariates), and both 1990–2000 parallel pre-trend tests and urban placebo falsification checks support causal identification of participatory community governance versus non-participatory municipal provision. Qualitative interviews and channel interaction models further corroborate the accountability mechanism.

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines participatory community management via water user associations, municipal user participation mechanisms, and grassroots social movements (participation); electoral accountability, political bargaining, and municipality–association coordination for state/federal grants (political_coordination, discretion); split urban/rural jurisdiction across state utilities (CESBs), municipalities, and associations (institutional_fragmentation); umbrella technical/organizational support programs such as CENTRAL, SISAR, and PROSAR (bureaucratic_assistance); urban-focused utility bylaws and pipeline-proximity rules excluding rural districts (ELIGIBILITY: service_area); community cost-sharing for internal pipes/meters and tariff concerns (BURDEN: fees); and administrative/funding application complexity (BURDEN: procedural_steps).
